units.translation: same as Γᾶ, Earth, Doric form
about which passage I have spoken under the word ἀλεύω.

to know, to have learned, to have found out, aorist infinitive of ἐδάην, from the unused present form δάω, of which certain other tenses exist, about which it has been said in the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 848. The tragedians used only the aorist ἐδάην and the participle δαείς.
But he forgets what he suffered and what he learned.
he learned the hare-devouring leaders of the procession

[which particle Aeschylus and Sophocles never used, is read in M. Pr. 933 τί δαί [what then?], where correctly in the apograph τί δ᾽ ἄν [what then would...], as the optative φοβοίμην [I would fear] requires. See Lexicon Sophocleum p. 109 a.]
having bound the man with a cunningly wrought robe
to cleave, to slay, to ravage
nor may any man-slaying pestilence come upon this city, ravaging it

where δαϊόφρων [woeful-minded] (luctificus, as Blomfield translates), is to be derived from δάϊος [wretched], as the measure of the first syllable shows, not, like δαϊκτήρ [lacerating], from δαΐζω [to cleave], as the scholiast believed, who explains it as δαΐζων τὰς φρένας [cleaving the mind]. More correctly the Byzantine scholiast says πολέμιος ταῖς φρεσὶ, λυπηρός καὶ διακόπτων τὰς φρένας ὁ θρήνος [hostile to the mind, grievous and cutting through the mind is the lament], although he too wrongly thought of the verb δαΐζω [to cleave], when he substituted διακόπτων [cutting through] for the participle δαΐζων [cleaving], which the old scholiast had used.
From the house a lacerating wail sends its sound to my ears, self-wailing, self-harming, woeful-minded, not loving joy.
hostile to the mind, grievous and cutting through the mind is the lament
before by the force of the lacerator he obtains the marriage of his heart
to be possessed by an evil spirit
I am possessed by an evil spirit
Alas, you who are maddened by ruin!
the house is maddened by evils
which seems rightly to be changed to δαιμονίαν [divine] by Westphal
Alas, divine ones, alas, curses of deaths that answer murder!
and no one (Auratus rightly reads οὔτις [no one]) arms the toilless (thus Pauw for ἄποινον [without recompense]) force of the divine ones,
divinity, of masculine or feminine gender
In the plural, of gods either all or many
most often it is said of a divinity, on whose will the fate of men depends, whether good or bad

θεοί [gods] and δαίμονες [divinities], although sometimes they are distinguished so that θεοί [gods] signifies the greater gods, δαίμονες [divinities] the lower divinities, about which it has been said in the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 860, nevertheless no less frequently these names are used without distinction of gods either all or individual, as
